interface_detail: a workflow YAML in .github/workflows; a runner with a shell and a network
tooling: a full Ubuntu, Windows or macOS runner with a shell, package managers and a checkout
chaining: a runner is a real machine for up to six hours, destroyed at the end of the job

limits.value: 'Each job in a workflow can run for up to 6 hours of execution time. If a job reaches this limit, the job is terminated and fails.' The row is headed 'All GitHub-hosted runners'.

'If a workflow run reaches this limit, the workflow run is cancelled. This period includes execution duration, and time spent on waiting and approval.' The threshold is 35 days per workflow run, so the workflow cap is 35 days and the job cap is 6 hours; the job cap binds first.
'The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes.' A schedule is also only honoured on the default branch.
'In a public repository, scheduled workflows are automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days.'
Job concurrency on the Free plan: 'Total concurrent jobs' 20, 'Maximum concurrent macOS jobs' 5, GPU 'Not applicable'. GitHub Support can raise it on a ticket.

No inbound reachability and no persistent disk. Quoted: 'When the job has finished, the VM is automatically decommissioned.' IPs are dynamic: 'GitHub-hosted runners use dynamically assigned IP addresses from shared infrastructure.'

The 'unlimited' is scoped by contract, not by meter. Quoted from the Additional Product Terms: 'If using GitHub-hosted runners, any other activity unrelated to the production, testing, deployment, or publication of the software project associated with the repository where GitHub Actions are used' should not be done. Also: 'Any activity that places a burden on our servers, where that burden is disproportionate to the benefits provided to users (for example, don't use Actions as a content delivery network or as part of a serverless application ...)'.

limits_note: The shape, the unlimited term, the 6-hour job cap, the 35-day workflow cap, the 5-minute cron floor, the 60-day schedule disablement and the 20-job concurrency are each quoted from a GitHub page read on 2026-10-24. The 6-hour cap is the one that binds: 6 hours x 20 concurrent jobs = 120 job-hours of wall clock, or 480 vCPU-hours, in any rolling window.
notes: The shape is confirmed exactly as the operator's answer states it: 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 14 GB SSD, workflow label ubuntu-latest, on a public repository, on an email alone. Two things the phrase 'free and unlimited' hides, and both were read on a page. First, the sentence is a vendor claim on a documentation page. The meter is unlimited, but use that the vendor judges disproportionate to the benefit to the project's users, such as a content delivery network or a serverless application, can be restricted, and no threshold is published at which it is safe: a worse ceiling than a number. Second, a figure of '14 GiB SSD' understates the vendor: GitHub writes 14 GB, decimal, which is about 13.0 GiB. The record keeps the vendor's number and unit. Not established: the egress term, which no page publishes; and whether enforcement of that restriction looks like a job cancellation, a repository disablement or an account suspension in practice. That would need a probe that has not been run.

free_tier.stated: On a public repository: 'Use of the standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited on public repositories.' The billing page repeats it as 'The use of standard GitHub-hosted runners is free: In public repositories / For GitHub Pages / For Dependabot.' On a private repository the GitHub Free plan gets 2,000 minutes a month instead. No card, no phone and no identity document is required for either. The word 'unlimited' is GitHub's own, and it is qualified by the Additional Product Terms, not by the billing page: see limits.
free_tier.notes: The unlimited half is the whole finding. The private-repo 2,000 minutes is the smaller half of the same account and a different product: 2,000 minutes is 33.3 hours of wall clock.

retention.stated: 'When the job begins, GitHub automatically provisions a new VM for that job. All steps in the job execute on the VM ... When the job has finished, the VM is automatically decommissioned.' Nothing on the VM survives the job. Artifacts and caches are separate services: caches are evicted after 7 days without access, capped at 10 GB per repository on GitHub Free.
retention.notes: 0 means the disk is destroyed at job end. Cache and artifact storage is a different service with its own clock.

egress.terms: not published on any page read: no egress quota, shaping tier or per-byte price is stated for a standard GitHub-hosted runner.

identity_cost.detail: 'To get started with GitHub.com, you need to have a personal account and a verified email address.' No phone: 'If you have been selected for mandatory 2FA, that does not mean you have to provide GitHub with your phone number.' No card and no hold, but this half is inferred rather than quoted, and the inference is stated: GitHub never writes 'no payment method is needed for public-repo Actions'. What the pages do say is that the card block is conditional on a quota being used up ('If your account does not have a valid payment method on file, usage is blocked once you use up your quota'), that public-repo standard runners are not billed at all, and that the always-charged products are the exception ('Larger runners are always charged for' and 'Usage of larger runners is always blocked until you set up a payment method'). A product that bills nothing has no quota to exhaust, so no card is demanded to use it. That is a documented absence, not a documented exemption, and it is one signup away from being settled.

RAM and disk are the vendor's decimal GB, kept unconverted: 16 GB is about 14.9 GiB and 14 GB is about 13.0 GiB. The private-repo default is a different shape: 2 vCPU / 8 GB / 14 GB.

session_cap.note: 6 hours per job on a GitHub-hosted runner, then the VM is destroyed and the job fails. 35 days per workflow run including queue and approval time. A scheduled workflow is the only way to start again, at a floor of once every 5 minutes, and it is disabled after 60 days without repository activity.

extras.price_arithmetic: USD 0.00 on a public repository. 24 hours a day is four 6-hour jobs, and the vendor charges nothing for standard runners on a public repository, so 4 vCPU x 24 h = 96 vCPU-hours a day at USD 0.00. With 20 concurrent jobs the ceiling is 4 x 6 x 20 = 480 vCPU-hours in any rolling six-hour window, and 4 x 24 x 20 = 1,920 vCPU-hours in a day if every slot is kept full. The private-repo alternative is 2,000 minutes a month = 33.3 hours of one job.

concurrency.note: GitHub Free plan, standard GitHub-hosted runners. GitHub Support can raise it on a ticket. 20 jobs x 4 vCPU = 80 vCPU at once, which is the number that turns one runner into a cluster.
